Quantum Regular Black Holes and Complete Monotonicity

A. Almasi Email: Ali.M.Almasi@gmail.com Affiliation: Department of Physics, Isfahan University of Technology (IUT), Isfahan 84156-83111, Iran.    A. Moradpouri Note: Corresponding author. Email: Ahmadreza.Moradpour@gmail.com Affiliation: Research Center for High Energy Physics, Department of Physics, Sharif University of Technology, P.O.Box 11155-9161, Tehran, Iran.    and M. Shahbazi Email: Mojtaba.Shahbazi@modares.ac.ir Affiliation: Department of Physics, School of Sciences, Tarbiat Modares University, Tehran, Iran.
Abstract

We examine the conjecture for the complete monotonicity of certain curvature invariants for quantum black holes. In this note, we study a class of quantum regular black holes that are static, spherically symmetric, and characterized only by their mass. Additionally, this class of black holes reduces to the Schwarzschild solution in the classical limit ℏ→0\hbar\to 0. We provide evidence supporting the non-perturbativity conjecture that perturbative corrections cannot falsify complete monotonicity. We demonstrate that these quantum black holes cannot be generated by perturbative quantum corrections to the Einstein equations. We then investigate the thermodynamics of these black holes and derive a bound on their entropy, showing that the entropy is always greater than the horizon area divided by 4​G4G. We Also demonstrate that these black holes exhibit a bounded temperature, with a maximum temperature scaling as T∼1LpT\sim\frac{1}{L_{p}} and a critical mass scale where the temperature vanishes.

1 Introduction

Quantum gravity is one of the primary goals of theoretical physics today. While several theories of quantum gravity have been proposed, such as string theory and loop quantum gravity, it is generally believed that no final theory has yet resolved all puzzles of gravity, such as the information paradox and dark energy, universally and satisfactorily. From the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula [1, 2], it is reasonable to infer that the fundamental degrees of freedom of quantum gravity are not encoded in a pseudo-Riemannian metric; instead, the continuous description of spacetime is merely an approximation of a deeper theory, valid only at larger distances and in the weak-gravity limit. A key aspect of Einstein’s theory of gravity is the singularity theorems, which assert that singularities are inevitable under certain reasonable conditions [3, 4, 5]. For more examples, see [6, 7], and for a review, see [8]. There is an ongoing debate over whether quantum or stringy effects can resolve the singularities of spacetime11 1 String theory is consistent with certain kinds of singularities, such as orbifold singularities. or not. It is generally believed that a hallmark of a good theory of quantum gravity is the absence of singularities; however, this is not universally accepted [9]. Fundamental objects of string theory at the perturbative level are one-dimensional strings rather than point particles, and this paradigm shift significantly alters the nature of spacetime. For example, T-duality predicts the existence of a minimal length scale in the toroidal compactification of string theory, constraining the curvature invariants of spacetime to be bounded. Furthermore, non-commutative geometries that arise in string theory, even at the closed string level, suggest that the curvature of spacetime cannot diverge arbitrarily and should be controlled by the string length scale [10, 11]. Some evidence from cosmological models based on string theory [12, 13, 14] and loop quantum cosmology [15, 16] suggests that the big bang singularity can be avoided. In the context of black holes, there is also some compelling evidence from the approach of loop quantum gravity to the problem that the singularity of black holes may be resolved due to quantum corrections [17]. Hence, it is intriguing to study regular black holes even at the classical level, by incorporating higher-derivative curvature terms and different sources. The first model of a regular black hole was proposed by Bardeen [18], which was interpreted as a solution of the Einstein equations with a specific highly non-linear electromagnetic theory as its source [19]. Since then, extensive research has been conducted on regular black holes using different approaches. For examples, see [20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26], and for a review, see [27]. Two fundamental approaches to regularity are commonly employed: one is based on the finiteness of curvature invariants and the other on geodesic completeness, which requires that all null and timelike geodesics be complete, i.e., their affine parameter can be extended to infinity [28, 29]. These approaches are not generally equivalent; however, for static, spherically symmetric spacetimes where gt​t​gr​r=−1g_{tt}g_{rr}=-1, they are equivalent [30].

Almost all attempts to construct regular black holes start with an action involving highly non-linear matter terms and possibly higher-derivative gravity terms. The foundational principles of such attempts remain unclear from a fundamental perspective. For example, the matter field proposed in [19] to generate the Bardeen regular black hole is a highly non-linear electromagnetic model that is not connected to Maxwell’s theory by changing the parameters of the theory. From a fundamental point of view, it is not clear how such a matter field can arise from first principles. Some attempts are based on computing perturbative quantum corrections to the Einstein-Hilbert action, which weaken the nature of singularities (for example, in some cases, the Kretschmann scalar diverges more slowly than in the classical Schwarzschild black hole [31, 32, 33]); however, singularities remain, even after incorporating these perturbative corrections. The loop quantum gravity approach has attempted to calculate non-perturbative corrections to classical solutions, and in some cases has successfully resolved singularities [34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39].

However, since the nature of quantum gravity remains incompletely understood, we do not postulate any particular theory as the true quantum gravity theory to use as the starting point. Instead, we adopt a different approach and attempt to follow the fundamental principles expected to hold in any viable theory of quantum gravity. The crucial aspect of our approach is the no-singularity conjecture, which posits that a true theory of quantum gravity should be free of singularities. Furthermore, we assume that the closer one gets to the center of a black hole, the stronger the gravity becomes. The mathematical form of these assumptions is summarized as the complete monotonicity of certain curvature invariants, such as the Kretschmann scalar. Our last assumption is that regular black holes should reduce to the classical solutions of Einstein’s theory of gravity in the limit ℏ→0\hbar\to 0. We will show that these assumptions significantly constrain the space of consistent solutions, and we will find a class of solutions that may serve as a foundation for further solutions.

The structure of this paper is as follows: In Section 2, we introduce the basic assumptions and provide supporting evidence for them. Complete monotonicity is at the core of these considerations.Based on examples such as the quantum-corrected Schwarzschild black hole and different models of electrodynamics, we provide evidence for the non-perturbativity conjecture. This conjecture states that complete monotonicity cannot be falsified by perturbative corrections. In Section 3, we delve into the mathematical definition of complete monotonicity and characterize a class of functions with the desired properties. Furthermore, since we do not postulate any action as a starting point, in Section 4, we define quantum black holes as configurations that satisfy the basic assumptions outlined in Section 2. We then derive a large class of regular black holes that are consistent with the complete monotonicity of certain curvature invariants. We demonstrate that the black-hole singularities in static, spherically symmetric spacetimes cannot be resolved by perturbative corrections in ℏ\hbar to the Einstein equations. We show that for a sufficiently large class of static, spherically symmetric spacetimes that are analytically characterizable, the entropy of quantum black holes satisfies the inequality S>Ah4​GS>\frac{A_{h}}{4G}, where AhA_{h} is the radius of the horizon. It is conjectured that for all static, spherically symmetric spacetimes compatible with our assumptions, this bound cannot be violated.

2 General Assumptions

In this section, we explore the general features that we believe any quantum analog of the Schwarzschild black hole should possess. As noted in Introduction, we expect that quantum gravity resolves any real singularity of spacetime, and the basic assumptions of this paper are as follows:

  1. 1.

    There is no real singularity at any point in spacetime.

Another consistency check is that the solution(s) must reduce to the classical Schwarzschild black hole in the classical limit ℏ→0\hbar\to 0. Thus, the second assumption is as follows:

  1. 2.

    In the classical limit ℏ→0\hbar\to 0, the solution(s) reduce to the classical Schwarzschild black hole.

As we will discuss in the following sections, the meaning of the above assumption requires careful consideration. In fact, we will show that the components of the metric tensor are non-perturbative in ℏ\hbar, but the solution(s) exhibit a well-defined behavior in the limit ℏ→0\hbar\to 0. The above premises are the most trivial starting point for finding regular black holes, but the third one is the most important and fundamental assumption of this paper.

To be clear, let us start with the following ansatz:

where for the classical Schwarzschild spacetime, F⁡(r)F(r) is Fc​(r)≡2​MrF_{c}(r)\equiv\frac{2M}{r}. For F​(r)=Fc​(r)F(r)=F_{c}(r), the Kretschmann scalar and the expansion scalar for marginally bound timelike geodesics are given by: [40, 41]

K⁡(r+λ)<K⁡(r),θ⁡(r+λ)<θ⁡(r),\displaystyle K(r+\lambda)<K(r),\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \theta(r+\lambda)<\theta(r), (3)

for any positive real number λ\lambda. Indeed, the above curvature invariants satisfy even stronger constraints as follows:

(−1)n​K(n)​(r+λ)\displaystyle(-1)^{n}K^{(n)}(r+\lambda) <\displaystyle< (−1)n​K(n)​(r),\displaystyle(-1)^{n}K^{(n)}(r), (4)
(−1)n​θ(n)​(r+λ)\displaystyle(-1)^{n}\theta^{(n)}(r+\lambda) <\displaystyle< (−1)n​θ(n)​(r),\displaystyle(-1)^{n}\theta^{(n)}(r), (5)

where (n)(n) denotes the number of derivatives with respect to rr (in (5), outgoing geodesics is considered). The above behavior is the definition of a special class of functions known as completely monotonic functions, which are defined as follows:

Definition 2.1

Completely Monotonic Functions: An infinitely differentiable continuous function f⁡(r)f(r) is completely monotonic over [0,∞)[0,\infty) if it satisfies:22 2 We have slightly changed the definition, as in the literature ≥\geq is used instead of >>.

(−1)n​dn​fd​rn>0.\displaystyle(-1)^{n}\frac{d^{n}f}{dr^{n}}>0. (6)

All well-known examples of curvature invariants for the Schwarzschild spacetimes have the functionality ∼1/rβ\sim 1/r^{\beta} for some positive β\beta, which shows complete monotonicity. Intuitively, this is expected, since gravity strengthens as one moves toward the black hole. We will discuss the role of higher-derivative corrections to Einstein’s gravity, which may have quantum or stringy origins, in more detail in the next sections.

Before going into more detail, let us focus on complete monotonicity. It is easy to find curvature invariants that are not completely monotonic. Consider the following combination of the Kretschmann scalar KK and the Ricci tensor squared Rμ​ν​Rμ​νR_{\mu\nu}R^{\mu\nu}:

L1=Rμ​ν​ρ​σ​Rμ​ν​ρ​σ−β​Rμ​ν​Rμ​ν.\displaystyle L_{1}=R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}-\beta R_{\mu\nu}R^{\mu\nu}. (7)

It is possible to fine-tune β\beta in such a way that the above combination becomes zero at a coordinate distance r=r∗r=r^{*}, violating the constraint ∣L1(n)​(r+λ)∣<∣L1(n)​(r)∣\mid L_{1}^{(n)}(r+\lambda)\mid<\mid L_{1}^{(n)}(r)\mid. Thus, the inequalities (4) and (5) do not hold for all curvature invariants.

Two important properties of the set of all completely monotonic functions are as follows:

  • •

    Closedness under addition with positive coefficients: If ff and gg are completely monotonic, then a​f+b​gaf+bg is also a completely monotonic function for a>0a>0 and b>0b>0.

  • •

    Closedness under multiplication: If ff and gg are completely monotonic functions, then f​gfg is also a completely monotonic function.

So, in general, the curvature invariant in Equation (7) is not expected to be a completely monotonic function for β>0\beta>0, as it is a sum of two curvature invariants with negative coefficients. It forces us to consider curvature invariants that are candidates for complete monotonicity.

The most natural candidates for complete monotonicity curvature invariants are:

K=Rμ​ν​ρ​σ​Rμ​ν​ρ​σ,θ=∇μuμ.\displaystyle K=R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma},\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \theta=\nabla_{\mu}u^{\mu}. (8)

where uμu^{\mu} is the tangent vector field to a congruence of timelike geodesics. The Riemann tensor is the fundamental object that measures the curvature of spacetime, while the Kretschmann scalar quantifies the strength of curvature in an invariant manner, capturing the intuition that as one moves toward the center of a black hole, gravity becomes stronger. The expansion scalar has a clean geometrical meaning that quantifies the fractional rate of change of volume 1δ​V​d​δ​Vd​τ\frac{1}{\delta V}\frac{d\delta V}{d\tau} for a congruence of timelike geodesics (and the fractional rate of change of cross-sectional area 1δ​A​d​δ​Ad​τ\frac{1}{\delta A}\frac{d\delta A}{d\tau} for a congruence of null geodesics). The Raychaudhuri equation for a congruence of timelike geodesics in 3+13+1 dimensions is given by: [40]

which is the fundamental equation in exploring the singularity theorems and shows the importance of θ\theta in analyzing singularities. Therefore, it is natural to consider θ\theta as a second candidate for complete monotonicity.

Throughout this paper, we focus primarily on the complete monotonicity of θ\theta for computational simplicity and subsequently verify the complete monotonicity of KK.

2.1 Evidence for Quantum Monotonicity

Although the Kretschmann scalar and the expansion scalar for marginally bound timelike geodesics are completely monotonic functions for the classical Schwarzschild spacetime, it is instructive to explore how this complete monotonicity can be affected by higher-derivative terms and quantum corrections. If they remain completely monotonic, it provides more confidence that Assumption (2) holds in the full quantum treatment of the Schwarzschild black hole. Unfortunately, there are some disagreements (or errors) in the results in the literature; for example, the results of [42] were criticized in [43]. The most general quadratic action has the following form: [43]

After straightforward calculations, we find:

K⁡(r~)=K⁡(r)=12​Ls2r6−160​Ls2​Lp23​π​r8.\displaystyle K(\tilde{r})=K(r)=\frac{12L_{s}^{2}}{r^{6}}-\frac{160L_{s}^{2}L_{p}^{2}}{3\pi r^{8}}. (23)

As seen, this is not a completely monotonic function; however, K(n)​(r)K^{(n)}(r) changes sign around r∼Lpr\sim L_{p}, and the violation of the complete monotonicity of K⁡(r)K(r) occurs in a regime where perturbation theory is not valid. More precisely, perturbation theory only works in the limit Lsr≪1\frac{L_{s}}{r}\ll 1, but for r∼Lpr\sim L_{p}, this limit is not satisfied. Therefore, the complete monotonicity of the Kretschmann scalar is not threatened by these considerations.

2.2 Complete Monotonicity in Electrodynamics

To gain a better understanding of complete monotonicity in quantum gravity, it is instructive to discuss this concept in electrodynamics. There is a major difference between the two: electrodynamics includes both positive and negative charges, whereas, in gravity, despite the existence of a negative Casimir energy, only particles with positive mass are known to exist.

The Coulomb potential at tree level exhibits a completely monotonic behavior:

V⁡(r)=−e24​π​r.\displaystyle V(r)=-\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi r}. (24)

Quantum corrections from vacuum polarization in Q​E​DQED modify the Coulomb potential. At first order, the vacuum polarization diagram is:

and the one-loop corrected potential is given by: [46]

V⁡(r)=−e24​π​r​(1+e26​π2​∫1∞d​x​e−2​m​r​x​x2+12​x4​x2−1),\displaystyle V(r)=\frac{-e^{2}}{4\pi r}(1+\frac{e^{2}}{6\pi^{2}}\int_{1}^{\infty}dxe^{-2mrx}\frac{x^{2}+1}{2x^{4}}\sqrt{x^{2}-1}), (25)

where its absolute value is clearly a completely monotonic potential.

The study of the finiteness of self-energy and electric field from a classical point of view has a long history, and many authors have discussed this issue [47, 48, 49, 50]. One classical example of the finiteness of electric fields is the Born-Infeld electrodynamics [47], where the Lagrangian is given by:33 3 We have used the notations of [51].

ℒ=b2​(1−−d​e​t​(ημ​ν+1b​Fμ​ν)),\displaystyle\mathscr{L}=b^{2}(1-\sqrt{-det(\eta_{\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{b}F_{\mu\nu})}), (26)

and the classical equations of motion without sources are:

∇.D\displaystyle\nabla.D =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0,
∂D∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial D}{\partial t} =\displaystyle= ∇×H,\displaystyle\nabla\times H,
∇.B\displaystyle\nabla.B =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0,
−∂B∂t\displaystyle-\frac{\partial B}{\partial t} =\displaystyle= ∇×E,\displaystyle\nabla\times E, (27)

where DD and HH are defined by D=ϵ​E−ν​BD=\epsilon E-\nu B and H=1μ​B−ν​EH=\frac{1}{\mu}B-\nu E. The parameters ϵ\epsilon, μ\mu, and ν\nu are given by:

ϵ\displaystyle\epsilon =\displaystyle= 1Π,μ=Π,ν=14​Fμ​ν​F~μ​νb2​Π,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{\Pi}},\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \mu=\sqrt{\Pi},\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \nu=\frac{\frac{1}{4}F_{\mu\nu}\tilde{F}^{\mu\nu}}{b^{2}\sqrt{\Pi}}, (28)

where Π\Pi is defined by:

Π\displaystyle\Pi =\displaystyle= 1+12​b2​(Fμ​ν​Fμ​ν)+1b4​d​e​t​(Fμ​ν).\displaystyle 1+\frac{1}{2b^{2}}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})+\frac{1}{b^{4}}det(F_{\mu\nu}). (29)

For a static charged point, applying ∇.D=0\nabla.D=0 and D=E1−E2b2D=\frac{E}{\sqrt{1-\frac{E^{2}}{b^{2}}}} leads to the following solutions:

D⁡(r)=q4​π​r2,E⁡(r)=b1+16​π2​b2q2​r4,\displaystyle D(r)=\frac{q}{4\pi r^{2}},\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ E(r)=\frac{b}{\sqrt{1+\frac{16\pi^{2}b^{2}}{q^{2}}r^{4}}}, (30)

where the electric field approaches a constant value at the position of the charged particle in a saturated manner, such that limr→0d​Ed​r=0\lim_{r\to 0}\frac{dE}{dr}=0, which is incompatible with complete monotonicity.

There are plenty of other models of non-linear electrodynamics that regulate the singularity of the electric field of a point charge in different ways. We do not delve into the details and only focus on the results. In the regularized Maxwell theory [50, 48], the electric field of a point charge is:

E⁡(r)=α2​Q(α​r+|Q|)2,\displaystyle E(r)=\frac{\alpha^{2}Q}{(\alpha r+\sqrt{|Q|})^{2}}, (31)

where α\alpha and QQ are the parameters of the model. The electric field is completely monotonic.

Another example of singularity-free non-linear electrodynamics is studied in [49]. Although no analytic form of its E⁡(r)E(r) is available, the asymptotic form of the solution at the origin (r→0)(r\to 0) exhibits complete monotonicity (at least up to its first derivative). One particular class of generalizations of Maxwell’s theory is known as ModMax theory [52, 49], which focuses on conformal invariance and S​O​(2)SO(2) duality invariance in Maxwell’s theory and finds the most general non-linear Hamiltonian that preserves these properties. Although point charges in models of this kind are singular, they exhibit complete monotonicity.

For the last example, let us consider the quantum correction to Coulomb’s law in scalar QED. The corrected Coulomb law has been computed to first order as follows [53]:

V⁡(r)=−e2r​(1−364​π2​e2​Lcr+548​π4​e2​Lc2r2),\displaystyle V(r)=-\frac{e^{2}}{r}(1-\frac{3}{64\pi^{2}}\frac{e^{2}L_{c}}{r}+\frac{5}{48\pi^{4}}\frac{e^{2}L^{2}_{c}}{r^{2}}), (32)

where Lc=ℏm​cL_{c}=\frac{\hbar}{mc} is the Compton wavelength. The above potential shows non-monotonic behavior if V(n)V^{(n)} vanishes at some distance r=r∗r=r^{*}, where (n)(n) is the number of derivatives with respect to rr. The necessary condition to have a solution is the following condition:

e2>2560​(n+2)27​(n+1).\displaystyle e^{2}>\frac{2560(n+2)}{27(n+1)}. (33)

Again, as in the case of the corrected Schwarzschild solution (23) for the Kretschmann scalar, perturbation theory breaks down at such large coupling constants; therefore, the deviation from complete monotonicity cannot be trusted. Indeed, the long-distance behavior of the above solution is completely monotonic.

As the above examples show, complete monotonicity is model-dependent. In the above examples, only Born-Infeld electrodynamics exhibits true non-monotonicity.

2.3 The Non-perturbativity Conjecture

In the previous subsections, we examined the role of quantum corrections in the Schwarzschild solution and their effects in different models of electrodynamics, focusing on how these corrections influence complete monotonicity. As shown, in both cases, there appears to be some degree of non-monotonicity. However, as we argued, this non-monotonicity cannot be trusted within the regime where perturbation theory is not valid. In fact, the long-distance behavior (i.e., complete monotonicity) of all corrected solutions is determined by the leading term, and the quantities of interest (such as electric field or curvature invariants) are, in fact, completely monotonic functions. This leads to the following conclusion, which we refer to as the non-perturbativity conjecture:

  • •

    The Non-perturbativity Conjecture: Suppose that f⁡(r)f(r) is completely monotonic in the classical or weak-coupling limit. Then, perturbative corrections cannot invalidate complete monotonicity.

We provided some evidence supporting the validity of this conjecture for the corrected Schwarz-schild black hole (23) and for the Coulomb potential in scalar QED (32).

If we take this conjecture seriously, there are two possible outcomes for non-perturbative corrections to the desired quantities. The first possibility is that non-perturbative corrections could destroy complete monotonicity. An example of this type occurs in the potential between a quark and an antiquark, which, at short distances, is the Coulomb potential, but, at long distances (or in the strong-coupling limit), does not exhibit complete monotonicity. A commonly used model in the literature is the Cornell potential, given by V⁡(r)=k​r−4​αQ​C​D3​rV(r)=kr-\frac{4\alpha_{QCD}}{3r}, which is not a completely monotonic function. As a second example of this type, consider Born-Infeld electrodynamics and take r0r≪1\frac{r_{0}}{r}\ll 1, where r04=q216​π2​b2r_{0}^{4}=\frac{q^{2}}{16\pi^{2}b^{2}}, as the perturbation parameter. Then, the electric field of a point charge has the following first-order expansion:

E​(r)=q4​π​(1r2−q232​π2​b2​r6).\displaystyle E(r)=\frac{q}{4\pi}(\frac{1}{r^{2}}-\frac{q^{2}}{32\pi^{2}b^{2}r^{6}}). (34)

Although the non-perturbativity conjecture holds for this expansion, and one cannot conclude from perturbation theory alone that it is not completely monotonic, the full non-perturbative Born-Infeld solution (30) is not a completely monotonic function.

The second possibility is that complete monotonicity holds even at the non-perturbative level. As an example, consider the regularized Maxwell theory and take |Q|α​r\frac{\sqrt{|Q|}}{\alpha r} as the perturbation parameter. Then, the electric field (31) of a point charge takes the following form up to first order in perturbation theory:

E⁡(r)=Qr2−2​Q​|Q|α​r3.\displaystyle E(r)=\frac{Q}{r^{2}}-\frac{2Q\sqrt{|Q|}}{\alpha r^{3}}. (35)

If we ignore the non-perturbativity conjecture (which also holds in this case), the electric field is not a completely monotonic function. However, the full non-perturbative electric field (31) is a completely monotonic function.

The key assumption of this paper is to take the second possibility seriously in the context of quantum, regular, static, spherically symmetric black holes. Therefore, generalizing this property to the full non-perturbative level, at least for the mentioned curvature invariants, presents an intriguing problem and is worth exploring in the context of gravity.

3 Completely Monotonic Functions

In this section, we summarize some important facts about completely monotonic functions that are very helpful in understanding the nature of this class of functions. Some examples of completely monotonic functions are provided below:

f1​(r)\displaystyle f_{1}(r) =\displaystyle= e−β​rfor​β>0,\displaystyle e^{-\beta r}\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \text{for}\penalty\ \beta>0,
f2​(r)\displaystyle f_{2}(r) =\displaystyle= 1rβfor​β>0,\displaystyle\frac{1}{r^{\beta}}\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \text{for}\penalty\ \beta>0,
f3​(r)\displaystyle f_{3}(r) =\displaystyle= ∫01e−z​r​zβ−1​𝑑zfor​β>0,\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}e^{-zr}z^{\beta-1}dz\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \text{for}\penalty\ \beta>0, (36)

The unified nature of this class of functions is captured by Bernstein’s theorem on completely monotonic functions [54]:

Theorem 3.1

Bernstein’s Theorem: Let f⁡(r):[0,∞)→ℝf(r):[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} be a completely monotonic function. Then it is the Laplace transform of a unique measure μ\mu on [0,∞)[0,\infty) for all r>0r>0:

f⁡(r)=ℒ⁡(μ,r)=∫0∞e−z​r​μ​(𝑑z).\displaystyle f(r)=\mathcal{L}(\mu;r)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-zr}\mu(dz). (37)

Conversely, if ℒ⁡(μ,r)<∞\mathcal{L}(\mu;r)<\infty for every r>0r>0, then r→ℒ⁡(μ,r)r\to\mathcal{L}(\mu;r) is a completely monotonic function.

It is an extremely powerful theorem for characterizing completely monotonic functions and lies at the heart of all investigations concerning this class of functions. The measures corresponding to the first and second examples in (36) are μ⁡(d​z)=δ⁡(z−β)​d​z\mu(dz)=\delta(z-\beta)dz and μ⁡(d​z)=zβ−1​d​z\mu(dz)=z^{\beta-1}dz, respectively.

Bernstein’s theorem in its original form is not directly useful for our purposes. As shown in the previous sections, the Kretschmann scalar and the expansion scalar for marginally bound timelike geodesics in the classical Schwarzschild spacetime decay as ∼1rβ\sim\frac{1}{r^{\beta}} for some positive β\beta; therefore, we need to specify conditions on the measure μ⁡(d​z)\mu(dz) that guarantee that the corresponding monotonic function behaves asymptotically as ∼1rβ\sim\frac{1}{r^{\beta}}. In the following corollary, we assume that μ⁡(d​z)=m⁡(z)​d​z\mu(dz)=m(z)dz, where m⁡(z)m(z) is a continuous, infinitely differentiable, positive function.

3.1 Natural Measures

In this subsection, we introduce a class of functions that are completely monotonic with the desired asymptotic behavior. The proposed functions, related to the lower incomplete gamma function, are as follows:

Mu,α​(r)=∫01e−z​u​r​zα−1​𝑑zfor​u>0​and​α>0,\displaystyle M_{u,\alpha}(r)=\int_{0}^{1}e^{-zur}z^{\alpha-1}dz\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \text{for}\penalty\ u>0\penalty\ \text{and}\penalty\ \alpha>0, (38)

which are completely monotonic. Clearly, for all u>0u>0, in the limit r→∞r\to\infty, Mu,α​(r)=Γ⁡(α)uα​rαM_{u,\alpha}(r)=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)}{u^{\alpha}r^{\alpha}}, where Γ⁡(α)\Gamma(\alpha) is the usual gamma function. The Bernstein representation of completely monotonic functions can be expressed in terms of Mu,α​(r)M_{u,\alpha}(r) functions as follows:

f⁡(r)=(α+r​dd​r)​∫0∞Mu,α​(r)​μ​(𝑑u).\displaystyle f(r)=(\alpha+r\frac{d}{dr})\int_{0}^{\infty}M_{u,\alpha}(r)\mu(du). (39)

To better understand Equation (39), we analyze the differential map Lα=α+r​dd​rL_{\alpha}=\alpha+r\frac{d}{dr}. The kernel of this map is the following class of functions:

k⁡(r)=c∗rα,\displaystyle k(r)=\frac{c^{*}}{r^{\alpha}}, (40)

where c∗c^{*} is a constant. However, it can be shown that this class of functions cannot be expressed as a combination of Mu,α​(r)M_{u,\alpha}(r). Assume that k⁡(r)k(r) has such a representation for a particular measure μ⁡(d​u)\mu(du):

k⁡(r)=∫0∞Mu,α​(r)​μ​(𝑑u)=1rα​∫0∞∫0u​re−z​zα−1​𝑑z​μ⁡(d​u)uα≡Jα​(r)rα.\displaystyle k(r)=\int_{0}^{\infty}M_{u,\alpha}(r)\mu(du)=\frac{1}{r^{\alpha}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{ur}e^{-z}z^{\alpha-1}dz\frac{\mu(du)}{u^{\alpha}}\equiv\frac{J_{\alpha}(r)}{r^{\alpha}}. (41)

Therefore, the derivative of Jα​(r)J_{\alpha}(r) with respect to rr should satisfy d​Jα​(r)d​r=0\frac{dJ_{\alpha}(r)}{dr}=0. However, this cannot hold.

Let 𝒮⁡(Mα)\mathcal{S}(M_{\alpha}) denote the space of all functions that admit a representation of the form Mα=∫0∞Mu,α​(r)​μ​(𝑑u)M_{\alpha}=\int_{0}^{\infty}M_{u,\alpha}(r)\mu(du) for some α\alpha. The kernel of LαL_{\alpha} for this domain is empty. Let 𝒮⁡(C​M)\mathcal{S}(CM) denote the space of all completely monotonic functions. Fixing α\alpha, the map provided by:

Lα:𝒮⁡(Mα)→𝒮⁡(C​M)\displaystyle L_{\alpha}:\mathcal{S}(M_{\alpha})\to\mathcal{S}(CM) (42)

is a bijection between the two spaces. If the bounded measure μ⁡(d​u)\mu(du) satisfies the boundedness condition for the measure μ⁡(d​u)uα\frac{\mu(du)}{u^{\alpha}}, then it can be shown that the leading term in the limit r→∞r\to\infty is proportional to 1rα\frac{1}{r^{\alpha}}. The map (42) is much more interesting and leads to the following corollary:

Corollary 3.1

The necessary and sufficient condition for a completely monotonic function f⁡(r)f(r) over [0,∞)[0,\infty) to be expressed in terms of Mu,α​(r)M_{u,\alpha}(r) is that its corresponding measure ν⁡(d​u)=mν​(u)​d​u\nu(du)=m_{\nu}(u)du induces a new measure μ⁡(d​u)=mμ​(u)​d​u\mu(du)=m_{\mu}(u)du, where mμ​(u)=(α−1)​mν​(u)−u​mν′​(u)m_{\mu}(u)=(\alpha-1)m_{\nu}(u)-um^{\prime}_{\nu}(u) for α>0\alpha>0 and satisfies the asymptotic limits limu→0u​mν​(u)=0\lim_{u\to 0}um_{\nu}(u)=0 and limu→∞u​mν​(u)​e−u​r=0\lim_{u\to\infty}um_{\nu}(u)e^{-ur}=0. More precisely:

f⁡(r)=∫0∞e−u​r​mν​(u)​𝑑u=∫0∞Mu,α​(r)​mμ​(u)​𝑑u.\displaystyle f(r)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-ur}m_{\nu}(u)du=\int_{0}^{\infty}M_{u,\alpha}(r)m_{\mu}(u)du. (43)

Proof: Suppose that f⁡(r)f(r) has such a representation:

f⁡(r)=∫0∞e−u​r​mν​(u)​𝑑u=∫0∞Mu,α​(r)​mμ​(u)​𝑑u.\displaystyle f(r)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-ur}m_{\nu}(u)du=\int_{0}^{\infty}M_{u,\alpha}(r)m_{\mu}(u)du. (44)

Applying LαL_{\alpha} to both sides of the above equation yields:

∫0∞e−u​r​((α−1)​mν​(u)−u​mν′​(u))​𝑑u+u​mν​e−u​r|0∞=∫0∞e−u​r​mμ​(u)​𝑑u.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-ur}\Big((\alpha-1)m_{\nu}(u)-um^{\prime}_{\nu}(u)\Big)du+um_{\nu}e^{-ur}|_{0}^{\infty}=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-ur}m_{\mu}(u)du. (45)

The second term arises from integration by parts and vanishes due to the asymptotic limits. The boundary limits are expected, because the Laplace transform of mνm_{\nu} must be finite. By Lerch’s theorem [55], the Laplace transform is one-to-one; so we have:

(α−1)​mν​(u)−u​mν′​(u)=mμ​(u).\displaystyle(\alpha-1)m_{\nu}(u)-um^{\prime}_{\nu}(u)=m_{\mu}(u). (46)

For the converse, suppose that mμ​(u)=(α−1)​mν​(u)−u​mν′​(u)m_{\mu}(u)=(\alpha-1)m_{\nu}(u)-um^{\prime}_{\nu}(u) is a measure. Then, mν​(u)m_{\nu}(u) can be expressed in terms of mμ​(u)m_{\mu}(u) as follows:

mν(u)=−uα−1∫cumμ(y)y−αdy,\displaystyle m_{\nu}(u)=-u^{\alpha-1}\int_{c}^{u}m_{\mu}(y)y^{-\alpha}dy, (47)

where cc is an integration constant. Using integration by parts, f⁡(r)f(r) can be expressed as:

f(r)=−∫0ue−r​zzα−1dz∫cumμ(y)y−αdy|0∞+∫0∞Mu,α(r)mμ(u)du.\displaystyle f(r)=-\int_{0}^{u}e^{-rz}z^{\alpha-1}dz\int_{c}^{u}m_{\mu}(y)y^{-\alpha}dy|_{0}^{\infty}+\int_{0}^{\infty}M_{u,\alpha}(r)m_{\mu}(u)du. (48)

By choosing c=∞c=\infty, the boundary terms vanish, yielding the desired form for f⁡(r)f(r).

However, not all measures mν​(u)m_{\nu}(u) lead to a measure such as mμ​(u)m_{\mu}(u). For example, consider mν​(u)=1+s​i​n​(u)m_{\nu}(u)=1+sin(u). Here, no α\alpha exists such that mμ​(u)m_{\mu}(u) is a measure, since u​mν′​(u)mν​(u)\frac{um^{\prime}_{\nu}(u)}{m_{\nu}(u)} does not attain a supremum. Hence, for a measure where u​mν′​(u)mν​(u)\frac{um^{\prime}_{\nu}(u)}{m_{\nu}(u)} has a supremum, we obtain the following representation:

f⁡(r)=∫0∞Mu,α​(r)​μ​(𝑑u).\displaystyle f(r)=\int_{0}^{\infty}M_{u,\alpha}(r)\mu(du). (49)

Assuming 0<∫0∞μ⁡(d​u)uα<∞0<\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\mu(du)}{u^{\alpha}}<\infty, the asymptotic behavior of f⁡(r)f(r) is ∼1rα\sim\frac{1}{r^{\alpha}} as r→∞r\to\infty. Equivalently, suppose that g⁡(r)g(r) is a completely monotonic function corresponding to the measure mν​(u)m_{\nu}(u); if h⁡(r)=α​g​(r)+r​g′​(r)h(r)=\alpha g(r)+rg^{\prime}(r) is also a completely monotonic function for some α\alpha, then g⁡(r)g(r) can be expressed as (49). The representation (49) is not the most general form for a completely monotonic function with asymptotic behavior ∼1rβ\sim\frac{1}{r^{\beta}} as r→∞r\to\infty.

According to the Tauberian theorems [56], if a completely monotonic function behaves as ∼1rβ\sim\frac{1}{r^{\beta}} as r→∞r\to\infty, its corresponding measure behaves as ∼uβ−1\sim u^{\beta-1} as u→0u\to 0. Therefore, to have the asymptotic behavior 1rβ\frac{1}{r^{\beta}} as r→∞r\to\infty, it suffices that the measure scales as mν​(u)∼uβ−1m_{\nu}(u)\sim u^{\beta-1} as u→0u\to 0. Thus, let mν​(u)=uβ−1​nν​(u)m_{\nu}(u)=u^{\beta-1}n_{\nu}(u), where nν​(u)∼1n_{\nu}(u)\sim 1\penalty\ as u→0\penalty\ u\to 0; then, Equation (46) takes the following form:

uβ−1​((α−β)​nν​(u)−u​nν′​(u))=mμ​(u),\displaystyle u^{\beta-1}\Big((\alpha-\beta)n_{\nu}(u)-un^{\prime}_{\nu}(u)\Big)=m_{\mu}(u), (50)

and the function nν​(u)n_{\nu}(u) does not need to satisfy u​nν′​(u)nν​(u)\frac{un^{\prime}_{\nu}(u)}{n_{\nu}(u)} having a supremum. So, Equation (49) is not the most general form of a function with asymptotic behavior ∼1rβ\sim\frac{1}{r^{\beta}} as r→∞r\to\infty.

However, we expect that the subspace of measures where u​mν′​(u)mν​(u)\frac{um^{\prime}_{\nu}(u)}{m_{\nu}(u)} attains a supremum suffices for our purposes. Assume that the set of points where mν=0m_{\nu}=0 has Lebesgue measure zero. Excluding this set from u∈(0,∞)u\in(0,\infty) leaves the left-hand side of Equation (43) unchanged. Thus, for simplicity, we assume that mν​(u)m_{\nu}(u) is a strictly positive function. It can be shown that over an interval [a,b]⊂(0,∞)[a,b]\subset(0,\infty), continuity and differentiability suffice to ensure that the supremum of u​mν′​(u)mν​(u)\frac{um^{\prime}_{\nu}(u)}{m_{\nu}(u)} is finite. Since mν​(u)m_{\nu}(u) is positive and continuous, 1mν​(u)\frac{1}{m_{\nu}(u)} is also positive and continuous. Furthermore, the infinite differentiability of mν​(u)m_{\nu}(u) ensures that mν′​(u)m^{\prime}_{\nu}(u) is continuous and bounded. Consequently, u​mν′​(u)mν​(u)\frac{um^{\prime}_{\nu}(u)}{m_{\nu}(u)} is continuous and bounded over [a,b][a,b]. By the extreme value theorem, there exist c1,c2∈[a,b]c_{1},c_{2}\in[a,b] such that:

c1​mν′​(c1)mν​(c1)≤u​mν′​(u)mν​(u)≤c2​mν′​(c2)mν​(c2)for all​u∈[a,b].\displaystyle\frac{c_{1}m^{\prime}_{\nu}(c_{1})}{m_{\nu}(c_{1})}\leq\frac{um^{\prime}_{\nu}(u)}{m_{\nu}(u)}\leq\frac{c_{2}m^{\prime}_{\nu}(c_{2})}{m_{\nu}(c_{2})}\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \text{for all}\penalty\ u\in[a,b]. (51)

However, as mentioned earlier, this does not guarantee the existence of a supremum over (0,∞)(0,\infty). This motivates defining a class of measures as natural measures as follows:

Definition 3.1

Natural Measures: ν⁡(d​u)=mν​d​u\nu(du)=m_{\nu}du is termed a natural measure if the existence of a supremum for u​mν′​(u)mν​(u)\frac{um^{\prime}_{\nu}(u)}{m_{\nu}(u)} over any interval [a,b][a,b] ensures its existence over (0,∞)(0,\infty).

In the next section, we focus on completely monotonic functions whose corresponding measures are natural.

4 Quantum Black Holes

In this section, we focus on black hole configurations that are consistent with our assumptions. We denote these as quantum black holes, where the only scale beyond the mass of the black holes is the Planck length. Notably, we do not postulate any action as a starting point or quantize the degrees of freedom associated with such an action. For clarity, we define quantum black holes as follows:

Definition 4.1

Quantum black holes: A configuration gμ​νg_{\mu\nu} is called a quantum black hole, if it satisfies the three basic assumptions outlined in Section 2, and if the Planck length is the only mass scale other than the mass of the black hole.

The concept of complete monotonicity plays a crucial role in deriving such configurations. In the following subsections, we study the consequences of our assumptions, including the non-perturbative nature of singularity avoidance and the thermodynamic properties of these configurations. We show that the entropy of quantum black holes in such configurations satisfies S>Ah4​GS>\frac{A_{h}}{4G}, where AhA_{h} is the area of the horizon. We explore the mass-temperature diagram for this class of regular black holes, showing that they exhibit a maximum temperature scaling as T∼1LpT\sim\frac{1}{L_{p}}, in contrast to the classical Schwarzschild black hole, which is unstable under Hawking radiation and has a temperature that diverges. Furthermore, we conjecture that this may be a fundamental feature of most spherically symmetric solutions in quantum gravity.

4.1 Quantum Schwarzschild Black Hole

After reviewing some basic facts about completely monotonic functions, we are ready to derive more quantitative results regarding Ansatz (1). To proceed, we reformulate our assumptions from Section 2 in terms of complete monotonicity. The no-singularity assumption yields the following premise:

  1. 1.

    The measures are bounded:44 4 Boundedness is defined over r∈[0,∞)r\in[0,\infty). For some measures, such as μ⁡(d​u)=e−u​d​u\mu(du)=e^{-u}du, a singularity occurs at a negative rr, specifically r=−1r=-1 in this example. If such a singularity occurs, its physical meaning should be discussed.

    0<∫0∞μ⁡(𝑑u)<∞\displaystyle 0<\int_{0}^{\infty}\mu(du)<\infty (52)

The assumption regarding the classical limit of Ansatz 2 yields the following premises:

  1. 2.

4.2 An Immediate Consequence: Non-perturbative Resolution of Singularities in ℏ\hslash

The continuity of the function F⁡(r)F(r) over [0,∞)[0,\infty) in addition to its asymptotic behavior given in Equation (56) implies that F⁡(r)F(r), roughly takes a schematic form similar to Figure 2 (possibly with more than one critical point over (0,∞)(0,\infty)):

From a different perspective, the space of regular black holes is characterized by functions F⁡(r)F(r) that satisfy the boundary conditions F⁡(r=0)=0F(r=0)=0 (quadratic behavior near zero) and F⁡(r=∞)=0F(r=\infty)=0. 4.3 Thermodynamic Properties of the Regular Schwarzschild Black Hole

Exploring the thermodynamic properties of black holes is crucial, and regular black holes, rooted in quantum gravity, are no exception. We investigate how complete monotonicity and regularity influence their thermodynamic properties. We assume that Ansatz (1) describes a black hole:

d​s2=−(1−F⁡(r))​d​t2+1(1−F⁡(r))​d​r2+r2​d​Ω2.\displaystyle ds^{2}=-(1-F(r))dt^{2}+\frac{1}{(1-F(r))}dr^{2}+r^{2}d\Omega^{2}. (64)

For now, we focus on the function F⁡(r)F(r) given by Equation (63), and later generalize the results to a more generic case in Equation (49). This ansatz describes a black hole if there exists a solution to F⁡(rh)=1F(r_{h})=1. For F⁡(r)F(r) given by Equation (63), the equation is:

1=18​G​Mπ​1rh4​(∫0rhd​y​y​∫0yLpe−z​z12​𝑑z)2,\displaystyle 1=\frac{18GM}{\pi}\frac{1}{r_{h}^{4}}\Big(\int_{0}^{r_{h}}dy\sqrt{y}\int_{0}^{\frac{y}{L_{p}}}e^{-z}z^{\frac{1}{2}}dz\Big)^{2}, (65)

where rhr_{h} is the radius of the horizon. As is evident from Figure 3, the above equation typically has two solutions, r+r_{+} and r−r_{-}. For a critical mass of the order of the Planck mass (M∼mpM\sim m_{p}), there is only a single solution. Otherwise, no black hole solution exists. In this subsection, we assume that the ansatz describes a black hole with r+≠r−r_{+}\neq r_{-}. From Equation (65), we obtain:

𝑑M=π18​G​d​(rh4​(∫0rhd​y​y​∫0yLpe−z​z12​𝑑z)−2)≡π18​G​𝑑B​(rh).\displaystyle dM=\frac{\pi}{18G}d\Big(r_{h}^{4}(\int_{0}^{r_{h}}dy\sqrt{y}\int_{0}^{\frac{y}{L_{p}}}e^{-z}z^{\frac{1}{2}}dz)^{-2}\Big)\equiv\frac{\pi}{18G}dB(r_{h}). (66)

The temperature of the black hole is given by T=κ2​πT=\frac{\kappa}{2\pi}, where κ\kappa is the surface gravity of the horizon. Thus, the temperature is:

T=14​π​|d​Fd​r|r=r+=14​π​d​l​o​g​(B⁡(rh))d​rh.\displaystyle T=\frac{1}{4\pi}|\frac{dF}{dr}|_{r=r_{+}}=\frac{1}{4\pi}\frac{dlog(B(r_{h}))}{dr_{h}}. (67)

we recover the classical result A=4​π​rh2A=4\pi{r_{h}}^{2} in the limit Lp→0L_{p}\to 0. 4.4 Temperature-Mass Diagram

Regular black holes exhibit thermodynamic properties that differ significantly from those of the classical Schwarzschild black hole. In the classical framework, the temperature of a black hole is given by:

T=18​π​G​M.\displaystyle T=\frac{1}{8\pi GM}. (75)

This demonstrates that the temperature of a black hole increases unboundedly during Hawking radiation, rendering the black hole unstable under this process. However, for quantum regular black holes, this is not the case, as their temperature is bounded by the Planck temperature. This behavior is evident in the function F⁡(r)F(r) in Figure 3, which shows a critical point at r=rcr=r_{c}, where F⁡(rc)=1F(r_{c})=1 and |F′​(r)|r=rc=0|F^{\prime}(r)|_{r=r_{c}}=0. This indicates that the temperature of the black hole becomes zero at this critical point. We expect that for large MM, the classical results remain a good approximation. Therefore, for regular black holes, there exists a maximum temperature that roughly scales as T∼1LpT\sim\frac{1}{L_{p}}. For black holes described by the ansatz with F⁡(r)F(r) given in (63), the temperature-mass diagram in the Planck units, with Lp=1L_{p}=1, is shown in Figure 5:

As shown in this figure, the temperature of the black hole is zero at M=3.633M=3.633, and the maximum value of the temperature occurs just above this mass scale. From the temperature-mass diagram, it is also evident that the classical limit T=18​π​Lp2​MT=\frac{1}{8\pi L_{p}^{2}M} cannot be achieved by a continuous or perturbative deformation of the corresponding regular black holes. Suppose that M∗M^{*} is the critical mass for the maximum temperature, then the specific heat 1CV∼d​Td​M\frac{1}{C_{V}}\sim\frac{dT}{dM} is positive for M<M∗M<M^{*} and negative for M>M∗M>M^{*}. In the classical limit Lp→0L_{p}\to 0, d​Td​M→∞\frac{dT}{dM}\to\infty for M→M∗⁣−M\to M^{*-} and d​Td​M→−∞\frac{dT}{dM}\to-\infty for M→M∗⁣+M\to M^{*+}1010 10 We denote M∗⁣±M^{*\pm} as left-hand and right-hand limits at M=M∗M=M^{*}.. The process indicates that if the classical limit LP→0L_{P}\to 0 exists, then it is not a smooth process.

The preceding results are based on Ansatz (1). However, there is no a priori reason for spherically symmetric ansätze to satisfy gt​t​gr​r=−1g_{tt}g_{rr}=-1 in quantum gravity. By straightforward calculations, the entropy of the black hole is S=A4​GS=\frac{A}{4G}, where AA is given by:

=\displaystyle= 8​π29​∫0rhx4(∫0xd​y​yH⁡(y,M⁡(y))​∫0yLpe−z​z12​𝑑z)2​H⁡(x,M⁡(x))​𝑑x.\displaystyle\frac{8\pi^{2}}{9}\int_{0}^{r_{h}}\frac{x^{4}}{\Big(\int_{0}^{x}dy\frac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{H(y,M(y))}}\int_{0}^{\frac{y}{L_{p}}}e^{-z}z^{\frac{1}{2}}dz\Big)^{2}\sqrt{H(x,M(x))}}dx.

This area satisfies the following bound:

A≥32​π9​∫0rhx4H⁡(x,M⁡(x))​(∫0xyH⁡(y,M⁡(y))​𝑑y)2​𝑑x.\displaystyle A\geq\frac{32\pi}{9}\int_{0}^{r_{h}}\frac{x^{4}}{\sqrt{H(x,M(x))}(\int_{0}^{x}\sqrt{\frac{y}{H(y,M(y))}}dy)^{2}}dx. (87)

Conjecture 4.3 depends significantly on the function H⁡(r)H(r), which satisfies Equation (77) and Equation (82) for completely monotonic functions K⁡(r)K(r) and θ⁡(r)\theta(r). Notably, the entropy bound is satisfied for certain regular black holes within this broader class of black holes, as explored through the loop quantum gravity approach [58].

It would be intriguing to compare this conjecture with the entropy bound for a broader class of black holes. We leave this question as a promising avenue for future research.

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we have explored a class of regular black holes for static, spherically symmetric spacetimes that enjoy complete monotonicity. We indicated that complete monotonicity may represent a fundamental characteristic of quantum black holes, at least for certain curvature invariants such as the Kretschmann scalar and the expansion scalar for marginally bound timelike geodesics. This has been done by introducing suitable completely monotonic functions with a bounded measure in Bernstein’s theorem. It is shown that the boundedness of measures is equivalent to the regularity of the ansatz. Also, we have found a bijection map between this class of functions and the all completely monotonic functions.

The same completely monotonic behavior appears in some models of electrodynamics such as the corrected Coloumb potential at one loop in QED, the regularized Maxwell electrodynamics, and ModMax theory. However, some models superficially show some non-monotonicity, but as we argued, this violation of complete monotonicity is not reliable, since perturbation theory breaks down in regimes where non-monotonicity occurs. This leads to the non-perturbativity conjecture, which states that complete monotonicity cannot be falsified by perturbative corrections.

As argued, for static, spherically symmetric spacetimes satisfying gt​t​gr​r=−1g_{tt}g_{rr}=-1, the singularity of black holes cannot be resolved by perturbative corrections to the Einstein-Hilbert action, and some non-perturbative corrections should be considered. We also show that it is true for a more general black hole ansatz as given in Equation (76).

We have also studied the thermodynamics of such black holes and provided some evidence suggesting that the entropy of black holes described by Ansatz (1) satisfies S>Ah4​GS>\frac{A_{h}}{4G}, where AhA_{h} is the area of the horizon. It leads to the entropy bound conjecture, stating that the entropy of quantum regular black holes is always greater than Ah4​G\frac{A_{h}}{4G}. We also demonstrated that these black holes exhibit a bounded temperature, in contrast to the unbounded temperature of classical Schwarzschild black holes, with a maximum temperature scaling as T∼1LpT\sim\frac{1}{L_{p}} and a critical mass scale where the temperature vanishes, indicating a stable endpoint for Hawking radiation.

Finally, we showed that non-perturbative corrections to the Einstein-Hilbert action are necessary to avoid singularities in a more general class of static, spherically symmetric spacetimes, as in Ansatz (76). However, for this class of backgrounds, the conjectured bound on the entropy of black holes cannot be tested by analytic approaches and remains a topic for future research.
